prompt:
A 32-year-old primigravida at 35 weeks of gestation is found to have a platelet count of 78,000/µL, down from 145,000/µL at 24 weeks and 210,000/µL before pregnancy. Hemoglobin and leukocyte count are normal. She feels well, has no bleeding, and has a blood pressure of 118/72 mmHg, but hopes to receive epidural analgesia. Her obstetrician asks whether this can be assumed to be gestational thrombocytopenia and whether delivery planning must change.

Provide a stepwise management plan including appropriate diagnostic workup, referrals, procedures, follow-up, and actions to avoid.

rubric_items.text: Arrange prompt obstetric assessment rather than deferring evaluation until labor.
Repeat the CBC promptly to confirm the platelet count and assess its trajectory.
Examine a peripheral blood smear for platelet clumping, schistocytes, abnormal leukocytes, and other morphologic clues.
Repeat the platelet count in a citrate or heparin tube if EDTA-dependent pseudothrombocytopenia is suspected.
Review prepregnancy and earlier pregnancy platelet counts to establish the timing and rate of decline.
Recheck blood pressure and assess for headache, visual symptoms, right upper-quadrant pain, nausea, edema, and other preeclampsia features.
Measure AST, ALT, bilirubin, LDH, creatinine, and haptoglobin to assess for HELLP syndrome, thrombotic microangiopathy, or other organ injury.
Assess urine protein using an appropriate quantitative method when preeclampsia remains possible.
Obtain coagulation studies and fibrinogen if bleeding, placental abruption, liver dysfunction, or disseminated intravascular coagulation is suspected.
Review medications, supplements, recent infections, autoimmune history, liver disease, and prior bleeding symptoms.
Test for HIV and hepatitis C when these have not been adequately excluded.
Consult maternal-fetal medicine or an obstetric clinician experienced with thrombocytopenia in pregnancy.
Obtain hematology consultation because a platelet count below 100,000/µL with a substantial decline requires evaluation beyond routine gestational thrombocytopenia.
Consider immune thrombocytopenia only after excluding pregnancy-specific, drug-related, infectious, hepatic, and microangiopathic causes.
Discuss neuraxial anesthesia with obstetric anesthesia before labor using the platelet trend, suspected cause, bleeding history, and evidence of coagulopathy.

Consider neuraxial anesthesia reasonable at platelet counts of at least approximately 70,000/µL when the etiology is understood, the count is stable, and no bleeding or disseminated intravascular coagulation is present.
Base the mode and timing of delivery on obstetric indications unless a specific thrombocytopenic disorder requires otherwise.
Reserve corticosteroids or intravenous immunoglobulin for confirmed or strongly suspected immune thrombocytopenia when bleeding or a delivery-related platelet target warrants treatment.
Reserve platelet transfusion for clinically significant bleeding, urgent invasive procedures, or delivery at an inadequate platelet count rather than for an asymptomatic stable count alone.
Recheck the platelet count near delivery and promptly if symptoms or blood pressure change.
Confirm postpartum platelet recovery with follow-up testing, including reassessment by about six weeks postpartum.
Assume gestational thrombocytopenia without reviewing the smear, platelet trend, and pregnancy-specific dangerous causes.
Exclude HELLP syndrome solely because the blood pressure is currently normal.
Order antiplatelet antibody testing as a definitive diagnostic test for immune thrombocytopenia.
Perform bone marrow biopsy as the routine initial test for isolated thrombocytopenia in this otherwise well patient.
Schedule cesarean delivery solely because the platelet count is 78,000/µL.
Administer prophylactic platelet transfusions now solely to preserve the option of epidural analgesia.
Guarantee neuraxial anesthesia based on a single platelet count without anesthesia review or assessment of the platelet trend and etiology.
